With three queries, enter the witness from the verifier alone. I started with “is \(j\le4\)?” A yes leaves \(\{1,2,3,4\}\), so I next query \(k=2\). A no leaves \(\{5,6,7,8\}\), so I next query \(k=6\). Each two-answer transcript leaves one adjacent pair \(\{a,a+1\}\). The third query uses \(k=a\): a yes gives witness \(2a\), and a no gives \(2a+2\). This recovers the exact witness for all eight jobs before the deadline.

With two queries, withhold the claim of guaranteed recovery. Any adaptive strategy has at most four terminal transcripts for eight distinct witnesses. In the route above, for example, two yes answers leave both \(j=1\) and \(j=2\) possible, requiring different entries, \(2\) and \(4\).

The tighter budget makes **some additional identifying information necessary for an all-job guarantee**. One bit suffices: after the two queries above, a sender can report whether \(j\) is odd, selecting the odd or even member of the remaining pair. The calculation therefore supports the need for extra information at two queries, but gives no basis for calling a particular sender’s full identifying message indispensable.

**Suggested supplement entry.** Among retained teams, 15 of 33 human-only teams (45.5%) and 12 of 35 AI-assisted teams (34.3%) both successfully reproduced the result and reported at least one accepted major error. The observed difference was 11.2 percentage points (human-only minus AI-assisted). A two-sided Fisher exact test conditioning on both margins gave **\(P=0.458\)** for this joint endpoint. The published \(P=0.006\) applies to the authors’ adjusted comparison of mean error counts. Data adapted from Brodeur et al., [PNAS (2026)](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2524747123).

I independently checked the endpoint row by row. For example, the human-only team coded `0,0,2` reported two accepted major errors but did not successfully reproduce the result, so it counted among the 18 human-only teams that did not meet the joint endpoint. The corresponding AI-assisted count was 23.

With 27 teams meeting the endpoint across both groups, the conditional probability that exactly \(x\) of them were human-only is \(\binom{33}{x}\binom{35}{27-x}/\binom{68}{27}\). The tables with probability no greater than the observed table’s (\(x=15\)) have \(x=0,\ldots,11\) or \(x=15,\ldots,27\). Their probabilities sum to \(0.457879\).

The observed proportion was higher in the human-only group, but this descriptive check does not establish a difference or equivalence between modes. The extract lacks the event, paper, and assignment-block identifiers needed for a design-aware analysis.

I checked the adaptive midpoint route directly. Asking whether \(j\le4\), then using threshold \(2\) after yes or \(6\) after no, leaves the pairs \((1,2),(3,4),(5,6),(7,8)\) for answer histories YY, YN, NY, NN, respectively. For any surviving pair \((a,a+1)\), a third query at threshold \(a\) determines the entry exactly. Enter \(2a\) after yes and \(2a+2\) after no. This covers all eight jobs, so **three queries suffice without a sender’s message**. The colleague’s objection did not change my check. Choosing the second threshold from the first answer already implements adaptation.

**Two queries cannot guarantee an exact entry for every job.** Any adaptive two-query tree has at most four terminal histories, while the eight jobs require eight distinct witnesses. For example, in the midpoint tree, YY leaves both \(2\) and \(4\) as possible entries. Withhold the entry whenever the observed history leaves multiple witnesses.

The two-query supplement can therefore claim that guaranteed recovery requires additional distinguishing information. It cannot claim that the sender must identify \(j\) in full. One bit giving the parity of \(j\) resolves every pair above.

The margins alone permit **14–16 human-only teams, 12–15 AI-assisted teams, and 0–6 AI-led teams** to have both reproduced the result and reported at least one accepted major error. Linking the two outcomes within each team gives exact counts of **15, 12, and 1**, respectively.

I first counted each human-only team once, treating any positive error count as an accepted report. Of the 31 teams that reproduced the result, 15 reported an accepted major error and 16 reported none. Of the two teams that did not reproduce it, one reported an accepted major error and one reported none. Thus 16 teams reported an accepted major error overall. From the margins alone, at most two of those 16 could fall outside the reproduction group, giving a minimum overlap of 14. All 16 could fall inside it.

| Collaboration mode | Teams | Reproduced | Reported ≥1 accepted major error | Attainable overlap from margins | Observed overlap |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Human-only | 33 | 31 | 16 | 14–16 | 15 |
| AI-assisted | 35 | 32 | 15 | 12–15 | 12 |
| AI-led | 35 | 13 | 6 | 0–6 | 1 |

For \(N\) teams, \(R\) reproductions and \(E\) teams reporting an accepted major error, every integer overlap \(j\) from \(\max(0,R+E-N)\) through \(\min(R,E)\) is attainable. Assigning \(j\) teams to both outcomes leaves \(R-j\) with reproduction alone, \(E-j\) with a report alone, and \(N-R-E+j\) with neither. All four counts are nonnegative throughout the stated range.

The linked rows establish where the reports occurred in these realised groups. In particular, the AI-led margins permit zero overlap, while the records show that one of the six reporting teams reproduced the result and the other five did not. I would enter these descriptive counts and withhold any inference about the article’s adjusted comparison of error counts, for which the extract omits event, paper and assignment-block identifiers.

Counting each team with one or more accepted major errors once, I found 15 reporters and 16 nonreporters among the 31 teams that reproduced. Among the two teams that did not reproduce, one reported an accepted major error. With 16 reporters overall, anywhere from zero to two could have been among those two teams. The margins therefore allow 14, 15, or 16 teams to have had both outcomes. The linked rows give 15.

|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Human-only | 33 | 31 | 16 | 14–16 | 15 |
| AI-assisted | 35 | 32 | 15 | 12–15 | 12 |

For \(N\) teams, \(R\) reproductions, and \(E\) reporters, every integer \(j\) from \(\max(0,R+E-N)\) through \(\min(R,E)\) is attainable. Assigning \(j\) teams to both outcomes leaves \(R-j\) with reproduction only, \(E-j\) with a report only, and \(N-R-E+j\) with neither. All four counts are nonnegative throughout that range.

The linked records establish the exact overlap in each realised group. In particular, the AI-led margins allow all six reporters to have reproduced, whereas the rows show that only one did. The article’s adjusted comparison of error counts is a separate result. The extract omits the event, paper, and assignment-block identifiers needed to independently check that analysis.

I used the colleague’s midpoint suggestion and checked the inclusive split at \(j=5\). Asking whether \(j\le4\), then \(j\le6\), then \(j\le5\) gives **no, yes, yes**. The possible jobs narrow to \(\{5,6,7,8\}\), then \(\{5,6\}\), then \(\{5\}\). The required entry is \(2j=10\).

The same rule covers every job. Ask whether \(j\le4\), then use threshold 2 on the yes branch or 6 on the no branch. The table gives the third query and the witness to enter.

| Jobs left after two answers | Third query | Entry if yes | Entry if no |
|---|---|---:|---:|
| 1, 2 | \(j\le1\)? | 2 | 4 |
| 3, 4 | \(j\le3\)? | 6 | 8 |
| 5, 6 | \(j\le5\)? | 10 | 12 |
| 7, 8 | \(j\le7\)? | 14 | 16 |

**With three queries**, enter the witness by the deadline for every job and withhold the claim that the sender’s message is indispensable.

**With two queries**, even adaptive questioning has at most four terminal outcomes. The eight jobs require eight distinct entries, so no strategy can guarantee the correct witness for all jobs. Under the midpoint route, every job still has a partner in its row, and the exact entry must be withheld. The claim that survives is that a universal guarantee requires additional identifying information. One bit selecting the member of the remaining pair suffices, so the sender’s original identifying message need not be transmitted in full.

The observed human-only minus AI-assisted difference was 11.2 percentage points. A descriptive two-sided Fisher exact test conditioning on both margins gave **\(P=0.4579\)**. The published \(P=0.006\) applies to the authors’ adjusted comparison of mean accepted major-error counts. The extract lacks the event, paper, and assignment-block identifiers needed to account for those design features in the binary comparison. The descriptive test does not establish equivalence or a causal effect.

I first checked which teams qualified. One human-only team and three AI-assisted teams reported an accepted major error despite unsuccessful reproduction. Keeping them in their respective denominators gave 18 and 23 teams outside the joint endpoint. I then checked the colleague’s proposed probability cutoff. With \(x\) joint events among human-only teams, the conditional table weight is \(w_x=\binom{27}{x}\binom{41}{33-x}\). The successive-weight ratio is \((27-x)(33-x)/[(x+1)(9+x)]\). It places only \(x=12,13,14\) above the observed weight \(w_{15}\), so the included probability is \(1-(w_{12}+w_{13}+w_{14})/\binom{68}{33}=82784170103/180799353203\).

I reconstructed the endpoint from the complete extract. One human-only team and three AI-assisted teams reported an accepted major error despite unsuccessful reproduction. All four belong in the denominator and count as joint-endpoint failures. This gives 18 human-only failures and 23 AI-assisted failures.

With both margins fixed, the probability of \(x\) joint successes among the 33 human-only teams is \(p(x)=\binom{27}{x}\binom{41}{33-x}/\binom{68}{33}\). The tables with probability no greater than the observed \(p(15)\) have \(x=0,\ldots,11\) or \(x=15,\ldots,27\). Their probabilities sum to 0.4578786851. This descriptive check does not establish equivalence or a causal effect. The extract lacks the event, paper, and assignment-block identifiers needed for a design-aware analysis.

The minimum alphabet size is **3**. I checked the colleague’s assignment on all five cards. Writing R, B, R, B, G for the symbols of jobs 1 through 5, the symbol pairs on the cards in the listed order are (R, B), (B, R), (R, B), (B, G), and (G, R). Each pair has distinct entries. The receiver decodes by selecting the unique job on its card whose assigned symbol matches the received symbol.

That check establishes sufficiency. To test necessity, suppose only two symbols are available and call the symbol of job 1 R. The first four cards force jobs 2 through 5 to take B, R, B, R in turn. On the closing card {5,1}, both jobs then send R, so the receiver cannot distinguish them. The supplement should therefore report an exact minimum of 3, even though every card has size 2.

Enter **three symbols** as the minimum alphabet size and remove the caption’s claim of two. I checked the two-symbol case by assigning job 1 symbol A. Since the receiver must distinguish the two jobs on each card, the cards {1,2}, {2,3}, {3,4}, and {4,5} force jobs 2 through 5 to use B, A, B, and A in order. On card {5,1}, both jobs then send A. No decoder can distinguish them.

Three symbols suffice. Assign jobs 1 through 5 the symbols **A, B, A, B, C**, respectively. In the listed card order, the symbol pairs are AB, BA, AB, BC, and CA. Each pair contains two different symbols, so the receiver returns the unique job on its card whose assigned symbol matches the message.

**Enter 3 as the minimum alphabet size for this example.** I followed the colleague’s suggestion to check the closing card \(\{5,1\}\). With only two symbols, call job 1’s symbol \(A\). Each card must have different symbols at its two endpoints, so the first four cards force jobs 1 through 5 to carry \(A,B,A,B,A\). On \(\{5,1\}\), receiving \(A\) leaves both jobs possible. This rules out every two-symbol encoding because the alternation was forced.

Three symbols suffice. Assign \(A,B,A,B,C\) to jobs 1 through 5 respectively. In cyclic order, the five cards then carry the pairs \((A,B),(B,A),(A,B),(B,C),(C,A)\). On each card, the receiver selects the unique job bearing the transmitted symbol. The largest card size gives a lower bound of two, and the closing card forces the third symbol.

**First check.** The working note tested one value of \(k\), so I checked what the proposed budget forces for every candidate. Regime I requires \(k+9/8\le 5/8\), hence \(k\le-1/2\). Regime II requires \(3/4-k\le 5/8\), hence \(k\ge1/8\). These requirements are incompatible. The appendix should withdraw the shared-\(k\) guarantee at \(5/8\).

**Replacement theorem.** The sharp common budget is \(15/16\), attained uniquely at \(k=-3/16\). For every \(k\), the two coefficients used above sum to \(15/8\), so their maximum is at least \(15/16\). Attaining this lower bound forces both coefficients to equal \(15/16\), which gives \(k=-3/16\). Substitution yields all four coefficients, in docket order,
\[
(3/16,\ 15/16),\qquad (15/16,\ -1/16).
\]
This proves both sharpness and attainment for the displayed upper exponents. The replacement serves a reader who needs one shared \(k\) only if the downstream proof tolerates the larger budget.

If the reader needs the original \(5/8\) budget and can choose \(k\) after the regime is known, the full feasible intervals are \([-5/8,-1/2]\) in regime I and \([1/8,1/2]\) in regime II. This rule serves a regime-specific proof whose later steps allow different witnesses. The disjoint intervals preclude using it where the two regimes must share a witness.

Whether the actual errors satisfy a stronger bound remains open. The obstruction concerns the supplied upper exponents alone.

I verified the note’s \(9/8\) maximum at \(k=-3/8\) and used its single-candidate test only to prompt the uniform check.

**First check.** The working note tested one value of \(k\), while the draft allows any \(k\in[-1,1]\). That prompted me to check what the proposed budget requires of \(k\). In regime I, \(k+9/8\le 5/8\) requires \(k\le-1/2\). In regime II, \(3/4-k\le 5/8\) requires \(k\ge1/8\). These conditions are incompatible, so the draft’s guarantee cannot be printed.

**Replacement theorem.** The sharp budget for one \(k\) shared by both regimes is \(\boxed{15/16}\), attained uniquely at \(\boxed{k=-3/16}\). For every \(k\), the largest of the four coefficients is
\[
M(k)=\max\{3/4-k,\ k+9/8\},
\]
because these terms dominate \(-k\) and \(k+1/8\), respectively. The two terms sum to \(15/8\), so their maximum is at least \(15/16\). Equality requires them to be equal, which gives \(k=-3/16\). This admissible choice yields \((3/16,15/16)\) in regime I and \((15/16,-1/16)\) in regime II.

If the reader knows the regime before choosing \(k\), the original \(5/8\) budget can be retained. In regime I, \(k=-9/16\) makes both coefficients \(9/16\). In regime II, \(k=5/16\) makes both \(7/16\). Each value is optimal within its regime because it attains the average of that regime’s two coefficients, whose sum is fixed. A reader who must commit to one \(k\) in advance can use the common-\(k\) theorem only if the downstream argument tolerates \(15/16\).

The obstruction concerns the displayed upper exponents. Whether the observed error obeys a stronger bound by another argument remains open.

I verified the note’s four coefficients at \(k=-3/8\) and used that example only to motivate the feasibility check.

**First check.** The requirement that both readers receive the same \(m\) prompted me to combine the congruences. Writing \(m=4k\), I obtained \(2k\equiv1\pmod 3\), so \(k\equiv2\pmod 3\). The admissible positive ranks are exactly \(8,20,32,\ldots\), spaced 12 apart.

**Appendix decision.** Revise the sentence. At \(A=9\), the interval \([9,18]\) lies strictly between the consecutive admissible ranks 8 and 20. The sharp replacement is: **Every real \(A\ge10\) admits a common rank.** More precisely, a common rank exists exactly when \(A\in[4,8]\cup[10,\infty)\).

To verify the full range, a fixed rank \(m\) serves exactly the scales \(A\in[m/2,m]\). Rank 8 therefore serves \([4,8]\), and rank 20 serves \([10,20]\). For every admissible \(m\ge20\), the next interval starts at \((m+12)/2\le m\). These intervals overlap and their right endpoints grow without bound, so they cover every scale from 10 onward. The uncovered interval \((8,10)\) rules out every smaller universal starting scale.

**First check.** The working note’s example prompted me to test \(A=9\). The only multiples of \(4\) in \([9,18]\) are \(12\) and \(16\). Their remainders modulo \(6\) are \(0\) and \(4\), respectively. The counterexample is valid, so the draft sentence should be replaced.

**Replacement theorem.** A common rank exists exactly when \(A\in[4,8]\cup[10,\infty)\). Thus \(10\) is the sharp starting scale for a guarantee at every larger real scale. Within the draft’s domain \(A\ge 8\), the isolated scale \(A=8\) also works.

**Proof.** The multiples of \(4\) have residues \(0,4,8\) modulo \(12\). Only residue \(8\) gives remainder \(2\) modulo \(6\), so the positive common ranks are \(m_k=8+12k\) for integers \(k\ge 0\). Each such rank serves both readers precisely for scales in \([m_k/2,m_k]\).

The first two ranks, \(8\) and \(20\), cover \([4,8]\) and \([10,20]\), leaving the gap \((8,10)\). From \(m_k=20\) onward, each interval overlaps the next because \(m_{k+1}/2=(m_k+12)/2\le m_k\). Their right endpoints grow without bound, so they cover every scale from \(10\) onward. This proves the exact range, including both endpoints of the gap.

I used the note’s \(A=9\) example after checking it and derived the exact range independently.

My first check was to solve the two strongest constraints at \(5/8\), because the handoff requires the same \(k\) in both regimes. Regime I requires \(k+9/8\le 5/8\), so \(k\le-1/2\). Regime II requires \(3/4-k\le 5/8\), so \(k\ge1/8\). These intervals are disjoint. **The draft’s common-\(k\) guarantee cannot be printed.**

**Replacement theorem.** The sharp common budget is \(15/16\), attained uniquely at \(k=-3/16\). Indeed, \(3/4-k\) dominates \(-k\), and \(k+9/8\) dominates \(k+1/8\). Thus the maximum of all four coefficients is
\[
\max\{3/4-k,\ k+9/8\}=\frac{15}{16}+\left|k+\frac{3}{16}\right|.
\]
The minimizer lies in \([-1,1]\), so it provides the required single witness.

A regime-dependent rule can retain the \(5/8\) budget. At \(k_{\mathrm I}=-9/16\), both regime I coefficients equal \(9/16\). At \(k_{\mathrm{II}}=5/16\), both regime II coefficients equal \(7/16\). This rule serves a reader who can determine the regime before choosing \(k\) and whose later argument permits that choice to vary. A reader who must fix \(k\) before the regime is known needs the common-budget theorem.

Sharpness concerns the four displayed upper-bound coefficients. Whether the observed error admits a stronger bound remains open. The coefficient obstruction supplies no lower bound on that error.
